caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Guyana's debt trajectory is the mirror image of its GDP explosion. The ratio fell from 74.5% in 2006 to 47.7% in 2007 on HIPC/MDRI debt relief, then drifted between 35% and 53% through the pre-oil decade (34.2% in 2019). Oil production then detonated the denominator: dollar GDP went from $5.47bn in 2020 to $8.04bn in 2021, $14.72bn in 2022, $24.66bn in 2024, and a projected $27.1bn in 2025 - roughly a fivefold increase in five years. Debt peaked at 47.4% in 2020, then collapsed to 24.8% in 2022, 24.3% in 2024, and a projected 28.6% in 2025. The government has wisely banked much of the windfall in the Natural Resource Fund (reformed in 2022) rather than borrowing against it. The risk is not solvency - it is Dutch disease and spending discipline as revenues keep rising.
inflation_management: Inflation has stayed remarkably contained given the scale of the boom, a credit to the Bank of Guyana's managed exchange rate and the NRF's sterilization of oil inflows. It spiked to 12.2% in 2007 and 8.1% in 2008 on global food and fuel prices, then ran mostly between -0.9% and 4.4% from 2009 through 2021, including outright deflation of -0.9% in 2015. The oil boom's demand pressures pushed it to 4.5% in 2021 and 6.9% in 2022, but it settled back to 2.8% in 2023, 2.9% in 2024, and a projected 3.3% in 2025. The central bank's challenge is novel: managing an economy growing at the world's fastest rates without letting construction, wages, and imports overheat - so far, the data say it is succeeding.

key_events.event: ExxonMobil's Liza discovery (May) opened the Stabroek block; one of the decade's great oil finds.
No-confidence vote toppled the Granger government, triggering a constitutional crisis.
First oil flowed in December; production began transforming the economy.
Disputed March election; Irfaan Ali (PPP/C) took office in August; COVID struck.
Natural Resource Fund reformed to govern oil-revenue saving and spending.
Maduro's December referendum on Essequibo escalated the territorial dispute; ICJ engaged.
Irfaan Ali re-elected September 1, 2025 (PPP/C 55.3%); production exceeded 600,000 bpd; GDP projected at $27.1bn.

outlook_next_decade: Guyana is the clearest structural growth story in the hemisphere: production is heading toward 1.2 million barrels per day by 2027, the NRF provides a fiscal buffer most oil states lack, and debt near 29% of GDP leaves enormous headroom. The base case is another decade of very rapid growth with rising per-capita income. The honest risks are governance of the windfall - whether oil money reaches the half of the population still in poverty - Dutch disease hollowing out agriculture and manufacturing, and the Essequibo dispute with Venezuela, which is the one tail risk that could upend everything. Watch NRF withdrawal rules: they are the single best indicator of fiscal discipline.
